newsitem.title: TANZANIA: United States calls for Burundi peace talks.
newsitem.headline: United States calls for Burundi peace talks.

text.p: Secretary of State Warren Christopher urged Thursday Burundi's warring parties to talk peace and said camps for Rwandan refugees in the region should be closed.
On the third leg of his first visit to sub-Saharan Africa, Christopher held talks with East African leaders in the northern Tanzanian town of Arusha ahead of a regional summit Saturday on Burundi.
Before leaving Arusha for South Africa, Christopher warned the international community should be ready to act to head off a humanitarian disaster if the situation in Burundi deteriorated.

"The United States calls on both sides in the conflict to suspend their hostilities and to begin all-party negotiations," said Christopher. The Tutsi-dominated Burundian army and Hutu rebels have so far set unacceptable conditions for peace talks.
"With good faith on all sides we believe a peaceful settlement is attainable.
"Should the situation in Burundi deteriorate further, however, the international community must be prepared to act quickly to prevent a humanitarian catastrophe," he added.
The international community, blamed for failing to act to prevent genocide in neighboring Rwanda in 1994, fears Burundi with the same ethnic mix could be plunged into similar bloodletting.
Ethnic civil war and massacres in Burundi have killed more than 150,000 people -- mostly civilians -- since October 1993.
The United States is pushing for a 10,000-strong African force to respond if Burundi sinks into genocide and Christopher said Tanzania had joined Mali and Ethiopia in offering troops.

Christopher spoke at a news conference after meeting Tanzanian President Benjamin Mkapa, Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi, Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni and former Tanzanian President Julius Nyerere, the international mediator on Burundi.
African foreign ministers meet in Arusha later Friday to decide whether to invite Burundi military ruler Pierre Buyoya, who seized power in a July army coup, to the Saturday summit.
Christopher said he had signs both sides in Burundi had expressed willingness to negotiate and cited Buyoya's decision to reopen parliament and lift a ban on political parties.
"When we see progress, we must be ready to recognize it. It is time for all sides to stop the killing and to start talking."

Diplomats said the United States believed Buyoya should come in person to Arusha to present his case to the presidents of Kenya, Uganda, Ethiopia, Rwanda, Zambia, the premier of Zaire and officials of the Organization of African Unity (OAU).
But Buyoya says he must be invited as the head of state.
The leaders will decide whether to ease, tighten, or lift an economic and transport embargo on Burundi since Major Buyoya ousted civilian Hutu president Sylvestre Ntibantunganya.

"I am in complete support of Buyoya coming to Arusha...It is important for him to come and give his ideas, program of action as well as listen to the views of individual heads of state," European Union special envoy Aldo Ajello told Reuters.
Diplomats said regional powers seemed divided on the issue with some countries led by Tanzania feeling inviting Buyoya would send the wrong signals of legitimacy to his Tutsi junta.
Christopher also said it was safe for the estimated two million Rwandan Hutu refugees who fled in 1994 to return to Rwanda and their camps in Tanzania and Zaire should be closed.

While in Arusha, he met the new chief prosecutor of the Internation Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, Justice Louise Arbour of Canada. Washington is giving the tribunal $650,000 in new aid to help prosecute mass rapes committed during the genocide.
